title: Day 87 · Week 12, Day 3 — Parents: the two of you — the small average drop and the sudden step at the birth, the childless couples who drift too, what a husband's fondness predicts, and the eight-class programme that changed the outcome in two trials
summary: What a first baby does to a couple, measured. Twenge 2003 (97 articles, 47,692 people): parents slightly less satisfied than non-parents (d = −0.19), largest for mothers of infants (38% vs 62% highly satisfied), explained by role conflict and restricted freedom. Mitnick 2009 (37 longitudinal studies): small declines to 11 months, moderate by 12–14 months — but childless newlyweds decline similarly. Lawrence 2008 (156 couples with childless controls): parenthood hastens decline; planning and pre-pregnancy satisfaction protect. Doss 2009 (218 couples, 8 years): a sudden, persistent, small-to-medium drop at the birth in mothers and fathers alike, against a gradual slope in non-parents. Shapiro, Gottman & Carrère 2000: a husband's fondness and awareness predicted mothers' satisfaction holding steady; negativity, disappointment and chaos predicted decline. The trials: the Cowans' couples groups (less decline over 66 months), and Family Foundations — coparenting classes before and after the birth — in 169 couples (coparental support, maternal depression and anxiety, infant regulation; effects to 3.5 years) and 399 couples (better on two-thirds of measures, large effects on family violence, most benefit for higher-risk couples). Pinquart & Teubert's 142-trial meta-analysis as the reality check (couple adjustment d = 0.13).
action: Tonight, ask your partner one question and only listen: 'What are you most worried will change between us after the baby comes?' No solving, no defending — a follow-up question or two. Then start a section called 'Us' in the pregnancy file and write one line with what she said.
